## What "multiclass" means here

A multiclass task predicts one of three or more classes that carry no order.
`uniml` treats it as a separate task type rather than as a binary problem with a
positive class bolted on, because almost every binary report is built around a
single event: a threshold, a positive class, a calibration curve, a decision
curve. None of those survives contact with four unordered classes without a
statement of convention.

What the package fixes for you is the convention:

| Quantity | Definition |
| --- | --- |
| `auc` | Hand and Till multiclass AUC: the mean over ordered class pairs of the AUC on class `i`'s own score column (`mlr3measures::mauc_au1u`) |
| `auc_ovr` | Macro one-vs-rest AUC: each class against the rest, then the unweighted mean; equals `mean(per_class$auc)` |
| `micro_auc` | Micro-average AUC: all (patient, class) pairs pooled into one binary problem |
| `brier` | Multi-class Brier score: mean over rows of the summed squared class errors |
| `logloss` | Mean negative log probability of the observed class |
| `sensitivity`, `specificity`, `ppv`, `npv`, `f1` | Macro averages of the one-vs-rest values |
| `micro_specificity` | Specificity pooled over the one-vs-rest cells |
| `balanced_accuracy` | Mean per-class recall, which equals the macro sensitivity |
| `kappa` | Cohen's kappa on the k-by-k table |

There is no micro precision, micro recall, or micro F1. For a single-label
multiclass outcome all three are identically the accuracy — the same number three
times — so the package reports accuracy once and says why. Micro AUC and micro
specificity are the two micro numbers that carry information of their own.

Every number is reproducible from the confusion matrix that comes with it, and
`tests/testthat/test-multiclass.R` pins them to `mlr3measures` and to a direct
recomputation.

## A worked example

`datasets::iris` is used here because it ships with R and has three classes; the
mechanics are the same for a clinical outcome with three risk groups.

```{r data}
library(uniml)

data <- iris
data$Species <- factor(data$Species)
table(data$Species)

spec <- uniml_spec(
  task_type = "multiclass",
  outcome = "Species"
)
spec <- set_learners(spec, c("cart", "rf"), tune = TRUE)
spec
```

Note there is no `positive`: a positive class only exists when there are two.

```{r task}
prepared <- as_uniml_data(data, spec)
levels(prepared$outcome)

task <- make_task(data, spec)
task$class_names
task$positive
```

## Train and score

```{r train}
learner <- train_model(
  task,
  mlr3::lrn("classif.rpart", predict_type = "prob")
)
prediction <- learner$predict(task)
head(prediction$prob, 3)
```

`calc_metrics()` recognises a prediction with more than two probability columns
and switches to the multiclass metric set:

```{r metrics}
metrics <- calc_metrics(prediction)
metrics[setdiff(names(metrics), c("confusion", "per_class"))]
```

The confusion matrix has the reference classes in rows and the predicted classes
in columns, and the per-class table turns it into one-vs-rest rates:

```{r confusion}
metrics$confusion
metrics$per_class
```

The macro sensitivity and the balanced accuracy are the same quantity computed
two ways, which is a useful check rather than a duplication:

```{r macro}
data.frame(
  sensitivity = metrics$sensitivity,
  balanced_accuracy = metrics$balanced_accuracy,
  accuracy = metrics$accuracy,
  kappa = metrics$kappa
)
```

## Does a model survive resampling?

Nothing here is special-cased for the workflow, so ordinary mlr3 resampling
applies; `calc_metrics()` scores the pooled out-of-fold predictions.

```{r cv}
resampling <- mlr3::rsmp("cv", folds = 5L)
resampling$instantiate(task)
cv <- mlr3::resample(task, learner, resampling, store_models = FALSE)

pooled <- as_uniml_multiclass(cv$prediction(), truth = cv$prediction()$truth)
cv_metrics <- calc_metrics(pooled)
round(cv_metrics$auc, 3)
round(cv_metrics$accuracy, 3)
```

Tuning works the same way as for a binary task, because the search space and the
resampling are mlr3 objects. `resolve_learners()` returns the package's learner
specifications, which carry their search spaces:

```{r tune}
learners <- resolve_learners(spec, task = task)
tuned <- tune_model(
  task,
  learners[["cart"]],
  resampling = mlr3::rsmp("cv", folds = 3L),
  tuner = "random_search",
  terminator = mlr3tuning::trm("evals", n_evals = 4L),
  seed = 123
)
tuned$status
tuned$best_params
```

## Comparing models

`rank_models()` averages a composite score whose metric set is declared by the
task type, so a multiclass comparison is not ranked on two-class numbers. The
multiclass composite is AUC, accuracy, balanced accuracy, and macro F1.

```{r rank}
score_row <- function(model, prediction) {
  values <- calc_metrics(prediction)
  data.frame(
    model = model,
    set = "validation",
    auc = values$auc,
    accuracy = values$accuracy,
    balanced_accuracy = values$balanced_accuracy,
    f1 = values$f1,
    stringsAsFactors = FALSE
  )
}

forest <- train_model(task, mlr3::lrn("classif.ranger", predict_type = "prob"))
comparison <- rbind(
  score_row("cart", prediction),
  score_row("rf", forest$predict(task))
)
comparison
rank_models(comparison, task_type = "multiclass")
```

A plain metric data frame carries no task type, so `task_type` has to be passed;
a `uniml_result` remembers it for you. Ranking a binary result is unchanged.

## Figures

Discrimination is shown as one-vs-rest ROC curves, one per class. There is no
single ROC curve for a multiclass problem, and averaging them into one line
hides exactly the class you are worried about.

```{r roc, fig.cap = "One-vs-rest ROC curves."}
binary_prediction <- as_uniml_multiclass(prediction)
plot_roc(binary_prediction)
```

```{r confusion-plot, fig.cap = "Confusion matrix: reference classes in rows, predicted in columns."}
plot_confusion(binary_prediction)
```

## Calibration

A multiclass model outputs a whole vector of probabilities for every patient, so
"is the number right" has to be asked in two ways. Both are reported, because a
model can pass one and fail the other.

```{r calibration}
calibration <- multiclass_calibration(prediction$prob, prediction$truth)
calibration$summary
calibration$per_class
```

* **Top-label** calibration keeps the largest probability of each row as the
  confidence and asks whether patients with 0.8 confidence really belong to the
  predicted class 80% of the time. Its numbers are `ece` (expected calibration
  error) and `mce` (the worst bin).
* **Class-wise** calibration repeats a one-vs-rest comparison for every class and
  averages the per-class ECEs without weighting, so a rare class that is badly
  wrong cannot hide behind the common ones. That is `ece_classwise`.
* `level_bias` is `mean confidence - accuracy`. It is the closest thing to the
  binary intercept: the multinomial model has no single slope to report, and its
  analogue (temperature scaling) is a recalibration method rather than a
  diagnostic.

ECE and MCE are bin-dependent summaries, not proper scoring rules; rank models on
the Brier score or the log loss, and read ECE as "how wrong is the stated
probability when the model is wrong".

```{r calibration-plot, fig.cap = "Reliability of the multiclass predictions: top-label confidence (left) and one-vs-rest per class (right)."}
plot_calibration(binary_prediction, scope = "both")
```

The same numbers ride along with every other metric, so they can be tabulated and
bootstrapped without a second call:

```{r calibration-metrics}
metrics <- calc_metrics(prediction)
round(metrics$ece, 3)
round(metrics$ece_classwise, 3)
metrics$per_class[, c("class", "ece", "mce")]
```

## What is deliberately missing

These are not gaps to be filled in later without a decision; each needs a
convention that a package should not choose silently.

* **Multiclass recalibration.** Platt scaling and isotonic regression are
  one-vs-rest by nature, and averaging `K` of them does not produce a calibrated
  multinomial distribution. The principled method is temperature scaling or
  Dirichlet calibration, both of which are recalibration methods the package does
  not implement yet; `calibrate_probabilities()` therefore refuses a multiclass
  probability matrix rather than shipping half of one.
* **Decision-curve analysis.** Net benefit compares one event against no event.
  Run one class against the rest with `as_uniml_binary()` and `dca()` if that is
  the question you are asking.
* **NRI / IDI, DeLong, Hosmer-Lemeshow.** All three are defined for a single
  positive class. They are not implemented for `uniml_multiclass`.
* **`run_workflow()`.** The full workflow is binary-only for now: its prediction
  table, thresholds, calibrators, and post-model tests all assume one probability
  column. Calling it on a multiclass specification stops with a message pointing
  back at this vignette. The layers underneath it are not binary-only any more —
  the task, the metrics, the calibration, and the composite ranking are all
  declared by the task type — which is why the pieces above can be combined by
  hand.

for multiple class classification problems. *Machine Learning*, 45, 171-186.

classification tasks. *Information Processing & Management*, 45(4), 427-437.

*Monthly Weather Review*, 78(1), 1-3.
